title: Privacy modern semantic transit system
subtitle: 1950-2026 routes from rights to data, platforms, surveillance, and AI-era privacy

routes.label: Rights / personhood
routes.description: Privacy as personal autonomy, private life, constitutional liberty, and legal rights.

routes.label: Information / data protection
routes.description: Privacy as information control, data protection, personal data, and governance duty.

routes.label: Internet / platform interface
routes.description: Privacy as web interface, policy notice, settings, consent screens, and platform defaults.

routes.label: Surveillance / security
routes.description: Privacy as a tension with policing, national security, monitoring, and mass surveillance.

routes.label: Breach / risk / compliance
routes.description: Privacy as operational risk, breach disclosure, compliance process, and institutional accountability.

routes.label: Identity / consent / advertising
routes.description: Privacy as identity control, consent, anonymity, trust, profiling, and targeted advertising.

routes.label: AI / biometrics / sensitive data
routes.description: Privacy as biometric, genetic, location, inference, and automated-decision concern.

stations.label: ECHR Article 8
stations.description: European rights language protects private and family life, home, and correspondence.

stations.label: Griswold v. Connecticut
stations.description: U.S. constitutional privacy becomes visible through marital and reproductive-rights reasoning.

stations.label: Reasonable expectation
stations.description: Katz reframes Fourth Amendment privacy around reasonable expectation rather than only property trespass.

stations.label: Fair information practices
stations.description: The HEW report helps consolidate fair information practice principles for computerized records.
stations.source_title: Records, Computers, and the Rights of Citizens

stations.label: U.S. Privacy Act
stations.description: Federal records privacy becomes a statutory administrative-control framework.

stations.label: OECD privacy guidelines
stations.description: OECD guidelines internationalize privacy principles for personal-data flows.

stations.label: Convention 108
stations.description: Council of Europe Convention 108 makes personal-data protection a treaty framework.

stations.label: Electronic communications
stations.description: Electronic communications privacy links communications networks, search, disclosure, and surveillance.

stations.label: EU Data Protection Directive
stations.description: EU privacy governance centers personal data, processing, and cross-border protection.

stations.label: Health privacy
stations.description: Health-information privacy becomes an institutional and sectoral compliance domain.

stations.label: Children online
stations.description: Children's online privacy turns consent, notice, and platform collection into a regulatory object.

stations.label: Security turn
stations.description: Post-9/11 security law intensifies the privacy-surveillance tension.

stations.label: ePrivacy / cookies
stations.description: European ePrivacy rules connect communications privacy, cookies, and online tracking.

stations.label: Breach notification
stations.description: California breach-notification law helps make data breaches a visible privacy-risk category.

stations.label: Privacy framework
stations.description: FTC consumer-privacy guidance ties privacy by design, simplified choice, and transparency to platform practice.
stations.source_title: Protecting Consumer Privacy in an Era of Rapid Change

stations.label: Mass surveillance
stations.description: Snowden disclosures make mass surveillance a global public-attention privacy frame.
stations.source_title: Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board archive

stations.label: GDPR adopted
stations.description: GDPR adoption consolidates personal-data rights, consent, accountability, and penalties.

stations.label: Platform profiling
stations.description: Cambridge Analytica and Facebook enforcement make profiling, consent, and social data visible privacy harms.

stations.label: GDPR applies
stations.description: GDPR enforcement begins and privacy becomes a mainstream product, policy, and compliance interface.

stations.label: Consumer privacy rights
stations.description: CCPA makes U.S. state consumer privacy rights and business obligations a mainstream privacy line.

stations.label: PIPL
stations.description: China's Personal Information Protection Law extends large-scale personal-information governance.
stations.source_title: Personal Information Protection Law of the PRC

stations.label: State privacy wave
stations.description: Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, and other state privacy laws broaden U.S. privacy compliance geography.
stations.source_title: California Privacy Protection Agency privacy resources

stations.label: AI and biometrics
stations.description: AI regulation brings biometric identification, sensitive inference, and automated profiling into privacy-adjacent governance.

visual_plan.route_layout: Use separate horizontal/diagonal route corridors with transfer stations at GDPR, consent, data breach, surveillance, and AI/biometrics.
visual_plan.animation: Use small moving dots along routes; do not animate station labels. Particle density can increase after 1995, 2013, and 2018 where data supports it.
visual_plan.interaction: Hover should resolve to fixed side-panel station details, not floating labels over the route map.

limitations: This is a chart-support data layer, not a complete global privacy-law database.
Google Books data ends at 2022, while the visual range runs to 2026; post-2022 flow should lean on anchors and attention metrics, not Ngram values.
Wikimedia pageviews are public attention proxies only and do not equal social importance.
Manual-review stations are useful for layout continuity but should be visually marked lighter until source-grade verification is complete.
Some legal sources are jurisdiction-specific; the metro metaphor should show branching semantic routes, not a single universal legal timeline.
